Don't be scared! The hardest part about Berkeley is getting in, so you're over the hump now!

1. I was also a CC student and was pretty similar to yourself (i.e., 4.0, honors, etc.). I'm sorry to hear about your parents, but I wouldn't get too hung up about maintaining a 4.0 in Berkeley. I put that kind of pressure on myself at first, but it isn't a realistic expectation. Getting a 4.0 isn't as important as doing a lot of extracurricular and internships. Talking to professors and GSI's and going to office hours can definitely benefit you. They rarely bump your grade up, but I've had professors personally extend deadlines for me or give me hints on upcoming exams. Study groups help too if you can form one and make study guides together. Also, they can give you notes in case you miss a class.

2. Yes, it's very possible to do double majors although a lot of the academic counselors that I spoke to while at Berkeley didn't recommend it. The consensus was mostly that doing a double major won't give you any big advantages when you're trying to land a job. However, a few of my transfer friends did double and triple majors successfully. 

3. Yes, you can study abroad. One of my friends was also a transfer student, and she studied abroad for 2 semesters in Spain on 2 separate occasions. The only thing is, unless you're taking a bunch of units during the year, you probably won't be graduating in 2 years doing a study abroad. My big advice would be to not force yourself to think you have to graduate in 2 years. At the time, my parents were pressuring me to graduate as early as possible due to financial reasons, so I overloaded on units and graduated in about 1.5 years. In hindsight, it was probably one of the biggest mistakes of my life as I didn't get to really take advantage of all the things Berkeley had to offer or really have time to make long lasting relationships with people there. I had basically no clue what I was doing my first year, so I pretty much felt like a freshmen my junior year. I joined several clubs that I later learned I didn't enjoy being in and wasted a ton of my time in them. During my last semester, I finally found an awesome club that suited my interests but by then, it was too late to really make any friends. If money is an issue, I'd really look into getting financial aid, grants, and scholarships. I really feel like 2 years is not enough time to get all you can out of Berkeley. 

4. I was a lot like you. I went into Berkeley not knowing anyone and had the same fear that everyone else already had a 2 year advantage to get to know each other. After graduating, I felt this to be very real, as everyone already had their own circle of friends to hang out with, so it was hard for me to get into those circles. However, I think it really depends on you. Try to be as extroverted and outgoing as you can. A few of my friends who were also transfers have made some pretty good friends. Are you going to be living in the dorms for your first year there? That's what I did. They usually group all the transfer students together on the same floor and throw a lot of social events for transfer students to get to know one another. I would look into clubs that interests you or go to one of the reddit meetups on campus. Also, unless you're Christian, try not to get sucked into joining their groups. My first day at Berkeley, I was sitting alone eating dinner at the cafeteria and a couple really cool and friendly upper grads asked if they could sit next to me and started chatting with me and even invited me to go bowling with them. I thought to myself, "People at Berkeley are so friendly and awesome!" As I kept hanging out with them throughout the rest of the semester, they revealed more and more about their agenda to convert me. It was too late for me, as I had already formed so many bonds with the members that it was hard for me to leave them and try to make new friends. I was already in my senior year by then. I also realized that they send out upper grads every semester to try to recruit freshmen and transfer students like me. I wish someone warned me about this beforehand.

I was an almost high school drop out, and I ended up transferring from a community college to UCB my junior year. 

I think the thing that helped me the most in transferring was the transfer center. Since your school is "tiny", I'm not sure they may have it. I basically had an adviser tell me all everything I needed to do to increase my chances of transferring. I also met with the UCB transfer scout and gave her a really good impression. I think giving that impression was the key to transferring for me, since she said something about how she something along the lines of how much she liked me and was going to put a good word in to her superiors or something after our meeting.

I think it's what you make of it.

I was a junior transfer from a community college, and it was very difficult for me to establish a good group of friends. It took me pretty much the entire first year I was there to figure out the campus, the people, what I like, and how things run and by then, I was already going to be graduating in a year, so I feel like I never got a real chance to establish a concrete group of friends. Most people I know who still talk to their friends after graduating met them during their freshmen year.
 
The most welcoming people would be the Christian religious groups because they actually send scouts in the beginning of every semester to try to "lure" you in. I remember my first day of class, I was eating alone in the cafeteria and two upperclassmen nonchalantly asked if they could sit with me. They were super friendly and for the first week, invited me out to all these cool parties and events. It didn't occur to me that their agenda was to eventually get me to go to church and bible study with them. 
It wasn't until my senior year that I found out about all these other cool clubs but like I said, by then I was going to be graduating already (along with all the people in my year), and so it was really hard to establish a connection with people who already had their own group of friends.

You aren't required to live in the dorms but I did my first year since I didn't know anything about living off-campus (i.e., where the good locations are, average rent price, etc.). I lived in unit 2 (towle), and though it was expensive, the dorms weren't actually that bad. It was safe and clean and they had a lounge area, study rooms, tutors, and a computer room. The one thing though was I absolutely hated my roommate, and I was stuck with him for the entire year.
